w:r.w:t: AI: Hardware-Aware AI Subtitle Generator with MFCC-Based Correction Validation and Embedding Self-Improvement for Low-Resource Indic Languages
Assistant Professor, Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering
Prince Shri Venkateshwara Padmavathy Engineering College,
Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering
Prince Shri Venkateshwara Padmavathy Engineering College,

Automated subtitle generation systems suffer from high Word Error Rate (WER) in noisy real-world conditions and exhibit particularly poor performance on low-resource Indic languages such as Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, and Hindi. Existing cloud-based tools degrade severely under background noise while providing no quality guidance to editors, and existing open-source tools offer no mechanism to validate user corrections against the underlying audio before storing them, creating a data quality risk for any self-improvement mechanism. We present

, a novel hardware-software co-design framework that integrates an ESP32 microcontroller as a dedicated Digital Signal Processing co-processor for real-time Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficient (MFCC) audio fingerprinting. The ESP32 implements a 512-point radix-2 FFT, 26-band mel
, and DCT-II entirely in embedded C firmware without any DSP library, producing compact 24-value audio fingerprints over USB serial within 200

. A Signal-Informed Quality Control module fuses Faster-Whisper ASR log-probability confidence with hardware-estimated Signal-to-Noise Ratio to generate RED and GREEN segment labels, reducing post-editing time by 61%. A privacy-preserving self-improvement loop stores hardware-validated user corrections as MFCC fingerprint–text pairs in a local SQLite database and applies them at inference time via nearest-neighbour cosine similarity lookup, requiring no GPU, no cloud infrastructure, and no model retraining. Experiments on 15 test videos totalling 4 hours 20 minutes demonstrate 91% correction validation accuracy, 90% QC classification accuracy (AUC = 0.89 vs 0.74 for ASR-only), and 23–26% relative WER reduction for Tamil and Telugu domain vocabulary after 30 minutes of correction data. The complete hardware addition costs Rs. 400–550.
AI provides a scalable, offline-first, and accessible subtitle solution for the 63 million hearing-impaired individuals in India.

Automatic Speech Recognition, MFCC Audio Fingerprinting, ESP32 Embedded DSP, Indic Languages, Signal-Informed Quality Control, Embedding Correction, Whisper, Hardware-Software Co-Design, Edge Computing, Subtitle Generation.

The rapid growth of digital content consumption across South Asia has made accurate, automated subtitle generation a critical accessibility and localisation requirement. Subtitles serve over 1.5 billion hearing-impaired individuals globally and are equally essential for multilingual content consumption in Tamil, Telugu, Hindi, Malayalam, Kannada, and other Indic languages spoken by over 200 million users in India alone who produce and consume educational, journalistic, and entertainment video content daily [10].
Commercial tools including YouTube Auto-Captions, Descript, VEED, and

achieve acceptable Word Error Rate in controlled studio conditions but degrade severely when background noise, fan hum, street traffic, or overlapping speech is present [4]. The WER for Tamil and Telugu speech processed by Whisper small in real-world noisy conditions has been measured at 42 to 65 percent, making automated subtitling unreliable without substantial human correction. This forces content creators to spend three to five times the video duration on manual correction, a bottleneck that disproportionately affects low-resource language content producers.

The correction process itself is entirely unguided in existing tools: all subtitle segments are presented identically to the editor regardless of their likely accuracy. An editor reviewing a 60-minute video must therefore watch the entire content to locate errors rather than being directed to the specific segments most likely to contain mistakes. This absence of quality guidance substantially magnifies the editing burden.

Two additional problems compound the situation. First, when a user types a correction in any existing tool, that correction is accepted without any acoustic verification that it matches the audio at the corresponding timestamp. A mishearing, a typo, or a language confusion can introduce an incorrect correction, and if the system attempts to learn from user corrections, bad corrections corrupt its improvement capability. Second, adaptation approaches for large ASR models such as Whisper typically require GPU hardware and hundreds of hours of labelled
training data per language [1], placing them out of reach for individual content creators, educators, and journalists in low-resource settings.

AI bridges these four gaps with three tightly integrated contributions: an ESP32 hardware MFCC co-processor for audio fingerprinting and correction validation; a Signal-Informed Quality Control engine combining ASR confidence and hardware SNR into RED/GREEN segment labels; and a GPU-free embedding correction self-improvement mechanism using SQLite nearest-neighbour fingerprint lookup. The complete system operates fully offline at Rs. 400–550 additional hardware cost.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work across ASR, subtitle generation, and audio feature extraction. Section 3 describes the proposed system architecture and its four functional layers. Section 4 presents implementation details. Section 5 reports experimental results and analysis. Section 6 concludes with future work directions.
2.1 End-to-End ASR Architectures and Confidence Estimation

The evolution of automatic speech recognition from Hidden Markov Model based systems to modern end-to-end neural architectures is comprehensively surveyed by Prabhavalkar et al. [1] in the IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing. The survey documents over 50 percent relative WER reduction attributable to deep learning and establishes that log-probability confidence signals from sequence-to-sequence decoders are systematically overconfident under distribution shift. This overconfidence is the primary motivation for augmenting ASR confidence with an independent hardware SNR measurement in
AI: when input SNR falls below 10 dB, ASR confidence alone is insufficient for reliable quality classification.

Radford et al. [2] introduce Whisper, a sequence-to-sequence Transformer trained on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised multilingual data, achieving near-human WER on clean English audio benchmarks. The

Their work confirms that Whisper adaptation requires GPU resources, large datasets, and extended training schedules—establishing the practical upper bound of what is achievable without these resources. Their validation of Faster-Whisper INT8 CPU inference benchmarks is directly referenced in
Reddy et al. [6] survey the evolution from HMM-based

deep learning ASR systems, confirming that MFCC features remain highly competitive with log-mel spectrograms for edge computing deployments due to their compact and noise-robust representation. This finding directly supports the choice of MFCC over raw spectrograms for the ESP32 fingerprinting component: the 12-coefficient MFCC mean vector is a 12-dimensional float array versus a 257-bin power spectrum, reducing both transmission bandwidth over USB serial and SQLite storage requirements.
Thara et al. [7] present a Whisper-based subtitle synchronisation system that corrects timing drift in pre-existing SRT files by comparing Whisper-generated word-level timestamps with

library. Their work validates that Whisper timestamp accuracy is sufficient for subtitle alignment tasks and confirms that Whisper word-level timestamp generation is the state of the art for subtitle boundary detection. Zhang et al. [10] demonstrate that segment-level ASR confidence combined with temporal alignment quality are the strongest predictors of subtitle editing effort, directly motivating the fused confidence score design in

Davis and Mermelstein [8] establish MFCC as the standard acoustic feature representation for speech recognition, documenting that the 12-coefficient configuration captures the most phonetically relevant spectral information with higher-order coefficients providing diminishing returns. Rezaul et al. subsequently validate that cosine similarity between MFCC mean vectors averaged across all frames of an utterance is a reliable metric for measuring acoustic similarity between audio samples of the same phoneme category, remaining robust to speaker variation and microphone gain differences. This validated property is the foundation of

AI's correction validation mechanism: two recordings of the same spoken word produce MFCC mean vectors pointing in similar spectral directions, yielding high cosine similarity regardless of recording volume.
No existing work in the surveyed literature combines hardware DSP quality estimation, acoustically validated correction storage, and GPU-free self-improvement for Indic language subtitle generation.
AI is designed as a four-layer hardware-software system. The architecture is illustrated in Figure 1 which shows the complete processing pipeline from video input to self-improved subtitle export.

The User Interface Layer is implemented as a

browser application running on localhost. It provides a left sidebar containing the ESP32 hardware connection status indicator with automatic port detection using the CP2102 USB vendor ID, a Whisper model size selector supporting tiny through large-v2, a language selector covering all 99 Whisper-supported languages with auto-detect default, and database statistics displaying per-language correction counts. The main area is divided into three tabs: Upload and Transcribe, Review and Edit, and Export. The Review tab displays each subtitle segment as a card with a RED or GREEN badge, segment timestamps, transcript text, fused confidence score, and its ASR confidence and SNR penalty components. RED segment cards include an expandable correction form with a Validate and Save button that triggers hardware re-fingerprinting. The Export tab provides SRT,
audio extraction, Faster-Whisper ASR transcription, Signal-Informed QC scoring, and embedding correction lookup.

extracts mono audio at 16,000 Hz from any MPEG-compatible video format and normalises it to a NumPy float32 array in the range [-1, 1]. Faster-Whisper processes the complete audio array with INT8 quantised inference using beam size 5 and Voice Activity Detection filtering with a 500-millisecond minimum silence threshold. For each returned segment, a 2-second audio clip is extracted with 100-millisecond boundary padding and sent to the ESP32. Before displaying any segment's transcription, the embedding correction lookup queries the SQLite database for stored corrections in the same language with cosine similarity above 0.80 and automatically substitutes the corrected text if a match is found.
The Hardware DSP Layer is implemented on the ESP32

v1 (dual-core Xtensa LX6, 240 MHz, 520 KB SRAM, 4 MB Flash) connected via USB-UART at 460,800 baud through the CP2102 bridge. Raw PCM int16 audio is transmitted using a binary protocol: two synchronisation header bytes 0xAA and 0x55 followed by a big-endian 16-bit unsigned sample count N followed by N times 2 bytes of signed 16-bit PCM samples. The firmware state machine transitions through WAIT_HEADER_1, WAIT_HEADER_2, READ_COUNT_HIGH, READ_COUNT_LOW, READ_SAMPLES, COMPUTE, and TRANSMIT states. A software MFCC fallback implemented using NumPy and SciPy activates transparently when the ESP32 is unavailable, producing identical output format.

When a user proposes an edit to a RED-labelled segment, the audio at that timestamp is re-fingerprinted by the ESP32. The combined similarity score between the original fingerprint vector μ₁ and the re-computed fingerprint μ₂ is:

Three outcomes are defined based on score thresholds: score ≥ 0.72 (HIGH: correction accepted and stored in SQLite with full metadata); 0.55 ≤ score < 0.72 (MEDIUM: accepted with secondary review flag); score < 0.55 (MISMATCH: warning displayed, explicit override required). Cosine similarity is the primary metric because it is invariant to absolute MFCC magnitude, making it robust to microphone gain variation between transcription and correction recording events, while remaining sensitive to the directional distribution of spectral energy that encodes phonemic identity.

Evaluation was conducted on a consumer laptop with Intel Core i5-1135G7, 8 GB RAM, no dedicated GPU, running Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. The ESP32
v1 was connected via USB-C to Micro-USB cable. Faster-Whisper small model with INT8 quantisation was used for all experiments. All evaluations were conducted offline without any network connectivity.

The test dataset comprised 15 video recordings: five Tamil, five Telugu, and five English. Tamil and Telugu videos included classroom lectures, documentary narration, and news broadcasts totalling approximately 4 hours 20 minutes across all 15 videos. Ground-truth transcriptions were prepared by native speakers for WER evaluation. For QC evaluation, 200 segments were manually labelled as correct or incorrect by native speakers. For correction validation, 150 test cases were prepared: 50 acoustically valid corrections where the corrected text matched the audio, 50 acoustically implausible corrections where the text was modified to a phonetically unrelated word, and 50 borderline cases involving phonetically similar word substitutions.

Table 3 reports WER across experimental conditions. Faster-Whisper small (INT8, CPU) achieves 29.4% baseline WER on Tamil clean audio and 33.1% on Telugu, consistent with benchmarks for Whisper small on low-resource Indic languages reported in [1]. After populating the embedding correction database with 30 minutes of validated corrections per language (approximately 180–220 correction records covering recurring domain vocabulary including speaker names, institutional names, and technical terminology), Tamil WER reduces

to 21.8% representing a 25.9% relative reduction, and Telugu to 25.4% representing a 23.3% relative reduction. English WER shows minimal change from 7.2% to 7.0% as English transcription accuracy is already high and fewer domain-specific corrections are needed.

The Signal-Informed QC engine was evaluated on 200 manually annotated segments where ground truth labels (correct or incorrect transcription) were established by native speaker review. The engine correctly identified 87 of 95 incorrect segments as RED (sensitivity 91.6%) and 93 of 105 correct segments as GREEN (specificity 88.6%), yielding overall QC accuracy of 90.0%. The fused confidence score achieves AUC = 0.89 in ROC analysis for RED segment detection, substantially outperforming ASR-only confidence (AUC = 0.74) and SNR-only thresholding (AUC = 0.71). This confirms the value of combining both signals: ASR confidence alone is insufficient at low SNR, while SNR alone does not capture cases where audio quality is
but the model produces low-confidence predictions due to domain vocabulary mismatch.

Editors reviewed only RED-labelled segments (approximately 35 to 40 percent of all segments), achieving the 61 percent overall editing time reduction. The 8.4 percent false-

negative rate (incorrect segments labelled GREEN) occurred primarily for moderate-noise segments where both ASR confidence and SNR penalty happened to produce a fused score just above the 0.75 threshold. Analysis suggests that lowering the threshold to 0.70 for Indic language content in noisy environments could improve sensitivity at the cost of slightly more segments requiring review.

On 150 prepared test cases, the ESP32 MFCC cosine similarity validator achieved 94% acceptance rate for acoustically valid corrections (47 of 50 classified as HIGH or MEDIUM confidence) and 92% rejection rate for acoustically implausible corrections (46 of 50 correctly flagged as MISMATCH), yielding overall validation accuracy of 91%. The 8% false acceptance rate for implausible corrections occurred exclusively for corrections involving phonetically similar word substitutions where MFCC fingerprints are genuinely similar despite lexical difference—an expected limitation of the spectral similarity approach that cannot be overcome without semantic information.

AI, a hardware-software co-designed framework for noise-robust multilingual subtitle generation with a specific focus on low-resource Indic languages. The system makes three original contributions to the subtitle generation domain. First, the
ESP32 hardware MFCC co-processor—with a 512-point radix-2 FFT, 26-band mel

, log compression, and DCT-II implemented from scratch in embedded C—provides audio fingerprinting for both quality control and correction validation at Rs. 400–550 hardware cost. Second, the Signal-Informed QC engine combining ASR log-probability confidence and hardware SNR achieves 90% quality classification accuracy (AUC = 0.89 versus 0.74 for ASR-only) and reduces editing time by 61%. Third, the hardware-validated SQLite embedding correction mechanism achieves 91% validation accuracy and provides 23–26% relative WER reduction for Tamil and Telugu domain vocabulary without GPU hardware or model retraining.
The system operates fully offline, supports all 99 Whisper languages with focused optimisation for Tamil, Telugu, Hindi, and Malayalam, and exports subtitles in SRT,
, and JSON formats. All hardware and software components are
with no licensing costs beyond the Rs. 400–550 hardware addition.
